A month ago I saw my first Opera: Lohengrin. The opera has on first glance a very Christian bias which I want to deconstruct here. If you are not familiar with the story, check out the Wikipedia entries about the character and the opera.

The tl:dr is the following:

Lohengrin is a knight of the holy grail and the son of Parzival, the grail king. One day the duke of Brabant dies and is left without a male heir. His daughter Elsa fears the kingdom will be lost, but Lohengrin arrives in a boat pulled by a swan and offers to defend her, though he warns her she must never ask his name. He weds the duchess and serves Brabant, but one day Elsa asks the forbidden question. He explains his origin and steps back onto his swan boat, never to return.

Wagner additionally adds the female and pagan Character of Ortrud, who wants to lure Elsa into asking the forbidden question by calling for the support of Wodan and Freia.. In the end it turns out the swan is the missing heir of Brabant who was bewitched by Ortrud. I will ignore this addition, as it is not a part of the original story.

Let's start with the story of Skeaf and Skild found in Schleswig/Slesvig. I only found a German version of the story here:

It says, that one day, when less people lived on this land, a ship without rudder and steersman was found. In this ship they found a sleeping naked baby boy, surrounded by weapons and treasures. The people saw that he was sent by the gods and educated him. Eventually they elected him to the first king of the Angles. His son was called Skild. Skild was long without a child, until at high age his son Beowulf was born. When the old king saw his death coming, he ordered to be put on a Ship and be let into the see, the same way he once came to this land. His people followed his wishes.

The parallel to the Swan Knight coming to help the damsel are obvious. Some people even suggest the hero and be traced back to Freyr himself.

But what about the swan?
The swan is a Valkyrie, as it is suggested in various bits the Edda. It also fits with both the wind and the Valkyries being "children" of Odin, but that might be a bigger stretch.

The forbidden question is more difficult, but already found in Greek Mythology in the story of Semele and Zeus. The relationship is ultimately sabotaged by Hera making Semela ask the forbidden question. This actually leads us back to Ortrud, which I actually wanted to ignore!

so tl:dr:

Lohengrin = sent by the gods, a god himself or a descendant of one
Swan = Valkyrie or Odin's child, the wind
Forbidden question = Semele, Zeus and Hera

And suddenly we both have a heathen story from the middle ages, and a heathen opera with a thin Christian coating! Maybe some people might now enjoy watching Lohengrin while applying an own "headcanon".

Trading, Sharing, Selling a used game is a one off tangible transaction. I buy a game, I have it it, I hold it, its mine to play or not play. When I'm done I can physically take it to someone else and give it to them or sell it to them or loan it to them, now they have it and I don't. Only one tangible copy is still in existence. Ethically it is no more sinister than lending a friend a vacuum cleaner.

Piracy on the other hand is exponential and virulent. It is day one. It isn't a loan, it isn't a sell, it isn't a gift, it is a copy, a duplication, two from one.

I've sold my games used and then later went and purchased another copy again because I wanted to play it again, that is a cost inherent in physical copies. When I give my copy away, if I want to play it again I will need to get another copy. Piracy does not have that cost/risk value. There is no initial sale, there is no risk in losing the copy, there is no cost in re-acquiring a copy. This is why it is ethically more damning.

The original creator should never factor in to used-item sales. Be it cars, vacuums, or physical media.

The way I see it is that there is a difference between entertainment media and usable objects. I buy stuff like vacuum cleaners, cars,... because I want to own and use them. Objects like these get made because people want to buy them. You rarely see overproduction because companies produce to meet the demand. As limited physical objects they inherently have a certain value.

In entertainment media this is different. There is no demand for particular games other than the demand the company artificially creates with things like trailers. One instance of a game/movie/song/book gets made and then it gets copied sold. They are pieces of information which can be copied infinitely so one particular copy of it has no inherent value. The value the information comes from the costs that it took to produce that information (mainly wages in most cases). When you buy a game you don't actually buy the game, you buy access to use the information of which the game consists. The disk you own and the information on it has essentially no value, the only reason to buy it is to support the creator of the information so he can continue producing things. With used games the seller has already used the information on the disk and then selling access to that information while he doesn't really have the right to give someone else access to information he doesn't own. If you sell your own copy and then buy someone else's copy afterwards, you still don't give money to the creators of the content. If you sell you own copy and then buy another copy from the creator, that's sort of equivalent to buying it for someone else.

Historically it was hard to restrict the access to a game to one person so publishers and console makers never bothered with it because it wasn't (and still isn't) a major problem. Microsoft tried to do it with the xbone, but there was a pretty big backlash against that so they gave up on the idea.
